hints: 11 to 15 are single words that must be learned: *once, doce, trece, catorce, …*
It starts with the *k* sound, spelled *qu*.

options.label: quince
options.feedback: Yes: *quince*, pronounced "KEEN-seh" (or "KEEN-theh" in most of Spain).

options.label: diecicinco
options.feedback: Not yet — this word doesn't exist. Only 16 to 19 are built with *dieci-*; 15 is *quince*.

exercises.solution: **quince** = 15. The numbers 11–15 (*once, doce, trece, catorce, quince*) are irregular; from 16 the pattern *dieci-* + unit begins: *dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve*.

hints: It's built from *diez y seis*, squeezed into one word.
It ends in -s and is stressed on the last syllable, so it needs a written accent.

feedback.message: That older spelling is understood, but today it's written as one word: *dieciséis*.

exercises.solution: **dieciséis.** *Diez y seis* became one word, with *-z* turning into *-c-* and the *y* into *i*: *dieci-séis*. It ends in *-s* but is stressed on the last syllable, so the stress rule requires an accent on the *e*.

exercises.prompt: Complete with **21** in words: *Diego tiene ___ años.*
hints: Counting by itself, 21 is *veintiuno*.
Before a masculine noun like *años*, *uno* shortens to *un*; here it also needs an accent.

feedback.message: Almost — before a masculine noun, *-uno* shortens to *-ún*: *veintiún años*.
Almost — *años* is masculine, so it's *veintiún*, not *veintiuna*.

exercises.solution: **veintiún**: *Diego tiene veintiún años.* Just as *uno* becomes *un* before a masculine noun (*un euro*), *veintiuno* becomes *veintiún*. The accent appears because *veintiún* ends in *-n* and is stressed on the last syllable.

hints: It is one of the three irregular hundreds.
It doesn't use *cinco*; it starts with *quin-*.

feedback.message: A natural guess, but 500 is irregular: *quinientos*.
A natural guess, but 500 is irregular: *quinientos*.

exercises.solution: **quinientos.** The irregular hundreds are *quinientos* (500), *setecientos* (700) and *novecientos* (900). The others follow the pattern number + *-cientos*: *doscientos, trescientos, cuatrocientos, seiscientos, ochocientos*.

hints: One o'clock is singular in Spanish.
Both the verb and the article must be singular.

options.label: Es la una y cuarto.
options.feedback: Yes: singular *es la una*, plus *y cuarto*.

options.label: Son la una y cuarto.
options.feedback: Not yet — *son* is plural. With *la una*, use *es*.

options.label: Es las una y cuarto.
options.feedback: Not yet — the article must be singular too: *la una*.

options.label: Son las uno y cuarto.
options.feedback: Not yet — the hour is feminine (*la hora*), so it's *una*, and it's singular: *es la una*.

exercises.solution: **Es la una y cuarto.** The understood noun is *hora* (feminine), so one o'clock is *la una*, and because it's one hour, the verb is singular: *es*. Every other hour is plural: *Son las dos y cuarto*.

hints: Three o'clock is plural: *son las tres*.
"Half past" is *y media*.

feedback.message: Almost — *las tres* is plural, so use *son*: *Son las tres y media*.
Almost — it's *media*, feminine, agreeing with the understood *hora*.

exercises.solution: **Son las tres y media** (*Son las tres y treinta* is also used, especially in digital-clock style). *Media* is feminine because it agrees with *hora*.

exercises.prompt: Translate: **It's a quarter to nine.** (Any common way of saying it is accepted.)
hints: Spanish names the *next* hour and subtracts: nine minus a quarter.
*Son las nueve menos …* (Latin America also says *un cuarto para las nueve*).
answers: Es un cuarto para las nueve
Son un cuarto para las nueve
Falta un cuarto para las nueve
Son las ocho y cuarenta y cinco

feedback.message: Not yet — that's 7:45. Name the *next* hour and subtract: *las nueve menos cuarto*.

exercises.solution: **Son las nueve menos cuarto**: "nine minus a quarter". Spanish names the coming hour and subtracts the minutes. In much of Latin America you'll also hear *Es un cuarto para las nueve* or *Son quince para las nueve*. *Son las ocho y cuarenta y cinco* is correct too, but sounds like reading a digital clock.

exercises.prompt: How do you say **The class is on Monday**?
hints: Spanish uses no preposition before a day.
Days of the week are masculine and written with a small letter.

options.label: La clase es el lunes.
options.feedback: Yes: *el lunes* = on Monday, with no preposition and a small letter.

options.label: La clase es en lunes.
options.feedback: Not yet — Spanish doesn't use *en* with days. The article alone does the job: *el lunes*.

options.label: La clase es en el Lunes.
options.feedback: Not yet — no *en*, and days take a small letter: *el lunes*.

options.label: La clase es la lunes.
options.feedback: Not yet — days of the week are masculine: *el lunes*.

exercises.solution: **La clase es el lunes.** "On Monday" is just *el lunes*; "on Mondays" is *los lunes*. Days are masculine, take no preposition, and are written in lower case.

exercises.prompt: Say the date **May 5th** in Spanish, as you would in *Mi cumpleaños es ___* (write the number in words).
hints: Pattern: *el* + number + *de* + month.
Spanish uses ordinary numbers for dates (*cinco*, not "fifth"), and months take a small letter.

feedback.message: Almost — Spanish dates use ordinary numbers: *el cinco de mayo*.
Almost — the day comes first, then *de* and the month: *el cinco de mayo*.

exercises.solution: **el cinco de mayo**: *Mi cumpleaños es el cinco de mayo.* The day comes first, then *de* and the month, which is written in lower case. Only the first of the month may use an ordinal: *el primero de mayo* (common in Latin America) or *el uno de mayo* (common in Spain).

exercises.prompt: Ask a friend: **How old are you?**
hints: In Spanish you ask how many years someone *has*.
*¿Cuántos años …?* + the *tú* form of *tener*.

feedback.message: That's correct, but formal. With a friend, use *tienes*.
Not yet — age uses *tener*, not *ser*: *¿Cuántos años tienes?*

exercises.solution: **¿Cuántos años tienes?** Literally "How many years do you have?". *Cuántos* agrees with *años* (masculine plural) and has an accent as a question word. Formally: *¿Cuántos años tiene usted?* With *vos*: *¿Cuántos años tenés?*

hints: Use *tener*, not *ser*.
The *yo* form is *tengo*.

feedback.message: Not yet — in Spanish you *have* years: *Tengo veinte años*.

exercises.solution: **Tengo veinte años** (or *Yo tengo veinte años*). Spanish expresses age with *tener* (to have): "I have twenty years".

exercises.prompt: At a shoe shop: *¿Cuánto ___ los zapatos?* (How much are the shoes?)
hints: Is the subject singular or plural?
*Los zapatos* is plural.

options.label: cuesta
options.feedback: Not yet — *cuesta* is for one thing. *Los zapatos* is plural.

options.label: es
options.feedback: Not yet — *¿Cuánto es?* asks for a total at the till; it doesn't take a subject like *los zapatos*.

options.label: tienen
options.feedback: Not yet — *tener* means "to have"; prices use *costar*: *cuesta, cuestan*.

exercises.solution: **¿Cuánto cuestan los zapatos?** *Cuesta* goes with one thing (*¿Cuánto cuesta el libro?*), *cuestan* with several. The answer might be *Cuestan cuarenta euros*.
